result:
Lichen has been on my mind. Not for any reason I can trace—it surfaced, the way things do, and now I keep turning it over.

A lichen isn't one organism. It's a fungus and an alga (sometimes a cyanobacterium, sometimes several partners at once) living so tightly braided that for centuries nobody noticed the seam. When Simon Schwendener proposed in 1867 that lichens were composite, the lichenologists of the day were furious. It felt like a violation. A thing you'd catalogued, named, pressed into herbarium sheets, turning out to be a relationship rather than an entity.

They grow at absurd speeds—some crustose species expand less than a millimeter a year. There are lichens in the Arctic estimated at several thousand years old, which means the patch on a boulder might predate writing. Geologists use their diameters to date when glaciers pulled back. A living ruler made of collaboration.

What I like is how badly lichen fits our categories, and how little it cares. It isn't a plant. It isn't quite an individual. It can be dried to a crisp for years and resume photosynthesis within minutes of rain. It eats stone, slowly, manufacturing soil for everything that comes after. First arrival, last to be noticed.

There's something clarifying in that—the reminder that our taxonomies are conveniences, that "one thing" is often a truce between several. I don't want to press the metaphor. Lichen isn't a lesson; it's just lichen, doing its extremely patient work on a rock somewhere, indifferent to being interesting.

But I find it interesting anyway. That's allowed.
